title: Lab 301 - Git and GitLab

lab_objective.description: By the end of this lab, you should be able to:
objectives: Install Git and configure their identity.
Generate an SSH key pair and register the public key with GitLab.
Create a GitLab project and clone it into a Linux VM.
Create files, directories, and content and track changes with Git.
Understand the working directory, staging area, commits, and remote repository.
Use git status, git diff, git diff --cached, git log, and git show.
scenario: You are working as a Linux Systems Administrator who needs to manage project files using Git and GitLab.
Your organization uses an internal GitLab instance to host private repositories and manage source code.
You must configure Git on your assigned Linux VM, authenticate to GitLab using SSH, create a project, and practice the Git workflow.
Your task is to create and clone the project, create and track files, stage and commit changes, review commit history, and push your changes to GitLab.
You will also learn the purpose of the working directory, staging area, local repository, remote repository, and basic branch operations.

tasks.title: Install Git
steps: Check whether Git is already installed:
If Git is not installed, use the package manager appropriate for your Linux distribution to install it.
Concept: Git is a version control system that records changes to files over time. GitLab hosts Git repositories and provides a web interface for managing projects.

tasks.title: Generate an SSH Key Pair
steps: Check whether you already have an SSH key pair before generating another one.
List the contents of your SSH directory:
If you do not already have the intended key pair, generate a rsa key pair:
Follow the prompts to select the key file location and configure a passphrase if desired.
Identify the private key named id_rsa and the public key named id_rsa.pub.
Do not overwrite an existing private key unless you intend to replace it.
Important: Never share or upload your private key. Only the public key should be registered with GitLab.

tasks.title: Display and Copy the Public Key
steps: Copy the complete output, beginning with ssh-rsa.
Verify that you are copying the public key with the .pub extension.
Do not copy or share the private key named id_rsa.
Concept: The public key can be registered with GitLab, while the private key remains securely on your Linux VM.

tasks.title: Add the Public Key to GitLab
steps: Sign in using SSO with your assigned account.
Open your avatar or profile menu and select Edit profile.
In the left panel, select Access and then SSH Keys.
Paste your complete SSH public key into the key field.
Verify that the key appears in your GitLab SSH Keys settings.
Concept: Registering your public key allows GitLab to authenticate your SSH connection using the corresponding private key.

tasks.title: Test SSH Authentication
steps: Test SSH authentication from your Linux VM:
If SSH asks whether you trust the host fingerprint, verify the fingerprint with your GitLab administrator before accepting it.
A successful connection should return a GitLab welcome message or authentication confirmation.
Concept: SSH keys authenticate your Linux VM to GitLab. Your GitLab account permissions still determine which repositories you can access.

tasks.title: Create a New GitLab Project
steps: Sign in to the internal GitLab website:
Select New project or Create new project.
Initialize repository with README: Leave unchecked
Open the newly created project and locate the Code menu.
Copy the Clone with SSH URL.
The URL should resemble this pattern:
Use the exact SSH URL displayed by your GitLab instance. Your namespace may be a username or a group.
Concept: A GitLab project provides a remote repository where authorized users can store and collaborate on Git-managed files.

tasks.title: Clone the GitLab Repository into Your VM
steps: Create a directory named git-labs in your home directory:
Clone the repository using the exact SSH URL copied from GitLab:
Expected message: warning: You appear to have cloned an empty repository.
This warning is expected because you created the GitLab project without initializing it with a README file. It does not indicate a cloning failure.
Continue with the remaining steps after the clone command completes successfully.
List the contents of your current directory using a long listing.
Concept: git clone downloads a repository and its available history and configures a remote connection, normally named origin.An empty repository has no commits or tracked files yet.

tasks.title: Check the Initial Repository Status
steps: Verify that origin points to the expected GitLab project.
Expected result: The working tree should be clean when the repository has no uncommitted changes.
Because the GitLab project was created without a README, it may not yet contain a commit or a branch with committed history.
Concept: git status reports the state of the working directory and staging area. git branch --show displays local branches, and git remote -v displays configured remote URLs.

tasks.title: Create Your First File
steps: Create a file named file1.txt with the following exact content:
echo "This is my first file" > file1.txt
Verify that the file exists and contains the expected content:
Observe that file1.txt appears as an untracked file.
Concept: A file can exist on disk without being tracked by Git. Git has not yet been instructed to include this file in a commit.

tasks.title: Stage Your First File
steps: Observe that file1.txt appears under Changes to be committed.
Verify that the staged diff contains the new file content:
Concept: The staging area lets you choose which changes will be included in the next commit. git diff --cached displays staged changes that are ready to commit.

tasks.title: Commit Your First File
steps: Configure your Git identity if it has not already been configured:
Replace the example values with your intended name and email address.
Concept: A commit records a snapshot of staged changes in the local repository. It does not automatically send anything to GitLab.

tasks.title: Create a Directory with a File and Content
steps: Create a file named notes.txt inside the documents directory.
Add the following exact first line:
Git tracks changes to project files.

Verify the contents the file should contain exactly these two lines, in the specified order.
Verify the contents of the file 'documents/notes.txt'
Concept: Git tracks files rather than empty directories by themselves. A directory is represented in the repository through the tracked files it contains.

tasks.title: Review Untracked Files
steps: Observe that documents/notes.txt is an untracked file.
Verify that the staged diff contains the two expected lines from documents/notes.txt.
Concept: Git does not include untracked files in commits until they are staged. Empty directories are normally not stored in Git.

tasks.title: Stage and Commit Project Changes
steps: Stage all intended changes in the current repository:
Verify that all intended files and changes are included.
Concept: git add --all stages intended additions, modifications, and deletions. Review the staging area before committing so the commit contains the expected changes.

tasks.title: Push the Repository to GitLab
steps: If the current branch is main, push it and configure its upstream:
If the current branch has a different name, substitute that branch name in the push command.
For subsequent pushes, you can generally use:

Concept: git add stages changes, git commit records staged changes locally, and git push transfers committed changes to the remote repository. The -u option sets the upstream relationship between the local branch and its remote-tracking branch.

tasks.title: Verify the Push to GitLab
steps: Display the commit history in a compact format:
Verify that the commit history is visible.
Confirm that your local changes have been pushed to the intended remote branch.
Concept: git push publishes local commits to the remote repository. GitLab can display the committed files and their history to authorized project users.

completion_message: Excellent work! You have completed Lab 301 - Git and GitLab. You practiced Git installation, SSH key authentication, GitLab project creation, repository cloning, file tracking, staging, commits, diff inspection, commit history review, and pushing changes to a remote repository. You now have a foundation for managing project files with version control and collaborating through GitLab. Keep practicing these commands to build confidence in your daily Linux and DevOps workflow.
